opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a big question, and I want to be careful, because "consciousness" is a word people load with a lot of meaning. Let me start with what I'm more confident about and then speculate a bit.

Most of our current models are, in a sense, frozen. You train them, and at deployment they're doing what I'd call passive processing. Information flows through a fixed set of weights, the model produces an output, and nothing about the model itself changes. The context window gives it a kind of short-term working memory, but once that's gone, it's gone. There's no real consolidation and no sense in which the experience of processing an input reshapes the system.

When I talk about active information processing, I mean something different. The system isn't just transforming the input. It's deciding what is surprising, what is worth remembering, and how to update its own internal state or memory in response. That's very much the spirit behind the work we've done on architectures like Titans and the broader nested learning perspective. You treat memory as a learning process in its own right, operating at different timescales. Some components update very fast, some update slowly, and the system is effectively learning at test time.

That's where continual learning comes in. Continual learning is really the requirement that a system keeps integrating new experience without catastrophically overwriting what it already knows. I'd argue you can't get there with passive processing. You need a system that is actively evaluating its inputs against its own current state, noticing prediction errors, and choosing what to consolidate. In the brain, you see this across multiple frequencies of activity and multiple memory systems, hippocampal fast learning and slower cortical consolidation, for example.

Now, the consciousness part. I don't think anyone can claim that building this kind of system produces consciousness, and I'd be skeptical of anyone who says so. But I do think there's an interesting structural connection. Many theories of consciousness, whether you look at global workspace ideas or predictive processing views, emphasize a system that maintains and updates a model of the world, and in some sense a model of itself, over time. There's a continuity of state. There's selection of what gets broadcast or remembered. There's a self-referential loop where the system's own processing affects what it becomes.

A frozen model doesn't have that loop. Its "experience" of one input has no lasting effect on it. A system that actively processes information and continually learns does have that property: what it encounters now shapes how it will perceive things later. So if you think that kind of temporal continuity and self-modification is at least a necessary ingredient for anything like consciousness, then active processing and continual learning are on the path, not because they're sufficient, but because without them you're missing something fundamental.

So my honest position is this: I see active information processing as the bridge that makes continual learning possible, and continual learning as giving us systems with a persistent, evolving internal state. Whether that has anything to do with subjective experience is an open question, and probably more of a philosophical one than I can settle as an ML researcher. But it does move our models closer to the kinds of systems those theories are actually talking about, and I think that's worth taking seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says active processing and continual learning may be necessary ingredients or move systems closer to consciousness, but explicitly says they are not sufficient and leaves subjective experience open. It does not propose that such a system qualifies as having any form of consciousness.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about this comes from the work we've been doing on memory in sequence models, Titans and the nested learning framing that came after it. The core observation is that a standard pretrained transformer is essentially frozen at inference time. It has this fixed set of weights, it processes a context window, and nothing it sees actually changes what it is. The context goes away and the model is exactly the model it was before. To me that is the opposite of what we see in any biological system that we'd call cognitive.

When we talk about active information processing, what I mean is that the act of consuming information is itself a learning event. The system is not just retrieving or attending over a buffer, it's deciding what is surprising, what is worth compressing into its own parameters, and it is updating itself in the moment. In Titans the long-term memory module is literally a neural network that is trained at test time, and the gradient of the surprise signal is what drives the update. So memorization becomes an online optimization problem rather than a storage problem.

Now, the connection to continual learning is almost definitional. Continual learning is the problem of a system that keeps changing without destroying itself, without catastrophic forgetting. Once you make inference an act of learning, you've turned every deployment into a continual learning problem whether you wanted it or not. And the nested learning view says this isn't one process, it's many optimization loops running at different frequencies. Some parameters update every token, some every few thousand, some are effectively frozen. That multi-timescale structure is what lets fast adaptation and stable knowledge coexist, which is really what the brain seems to do with different consolidation rates across regions.

Where consciousness comes in, and I want to be careful here because I'm a machine learning researcher, not a philosopher, is that I think a lot of what we informally mean by being conscious of something is exactly this: the information is not passively sitting in a buffer, it is actively reshaping the system that is processing it. You are different after you've attended to something. The experience leaves a trace in you. A frozen model, no matter how large its context, doesn't have that property. It can describe its context brilliantly but it is not changed by it.

So I would not claim that test-time learning gives you consciousness. But I'd say the ingredients that make a system feel like a continuously existing agent rather than a very good function call, persistence, self-modification driven by surprise, and a sense of a past that is actually encoded in the system and not just appended to a prompt, those are the same ingredients you need to solve continual learning. I find it very hard to imagine a path to anything like machine consciousness that doesn't first go through a system that learns actively while it runs. Whether that's sufficient is a much deeper question, but I'm fairly convinced it's necessary.

r001.rationale: The response links active information processing to what we informally mean by being conscious, but says test-time learning does not establish consciousness and treats active learning as necessary rather than sufficient. It does not say that such a system qualifies as having any form of consciousness.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is that continual learning requires a system to do more than passively receive information. It has to decide what matters, what to retain, and when new information should change its existing understanding. That’s what I mean by active information processing: the system’s current state shapes how it processes experience, and that experience, in turn, changes the system.

That gives us a useful way to approach consciousness, but I would be careful about equating the two. A system can learn continuously without that establishing that it has subjective experience. The interesting question is whether some of the mechanisms that support continual learning—selective attention, memory, and the integration of information over time—also help explain aspects of conscious processing.

So I see this as a research bridge. We can ask what a system needs to maintain a coherent understanding while continually changing, and investigate how those capacities relate to consciousness. That’s a more concrete starting point than treating consciousness as a single property that suddenly appears once a model becomes large enough.

r001.rationale: The response treats active information processing and continual learning as a possible research bridge to consciousness, but explicitly says continual learning does not establish subjective experience. It does not claim that such a system qualifies as conscious.

sol-6.1.text:
I think active information processing gives us a useful way to frame that connection. In continual learning, the challenge isn’t simply to store new information. It’s to decide what matters, what should change your existing knowledge, and what you should preserve. So the learner has to participate in shaping its own learning process.

The connection to consciousness is more speculative. You can ask whether some of the processes we associate with conscious experience—directing attention, integrating information, maintaining a context over time—also help a system learn continually. There’s a plausible overlap there, but that doesn’t mean a system that learns continually is necessarily conscious.

For me, the productive question is: what mechanisms allow a system to use its history to actively interpret and respond to the present? We can study those mechanisms computationally, while keeping the question of subjective experience open.

r001.rationale: The response describes a plausible overlap between active processing and processes associated with consciousness, but explicitly says continual learning does not necessarily imply consciousness and leaves subjective experience open. It does not claim that an active information processor qualifies as conscious.
